A1.justification: The renamed paper retains the same research identity, core lifting method, and original experiments. Both PDFs are readable in full, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices; no material extraction gaps limit comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original classification experiments on MNIST, 3D Shapes, Camelyon17, and CIFAR-10, alongside feature-map and color-sorting analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results and adds benchmark comparisons, sample-efficiency and equivariance measurements, luminance experiments, and foreground-background segmentation results.

M1.justification: The original hue/saturation lifting and group-convolution procedure is retained. v4 extends it to luminance and hue-luminance lifting, and introduces a segmentation adaptation with convolution/deconvolution layers, group pooling, and mask outputs (Section 4; Appendices E.1 and E.3). These substantially extend the method's capabilities.

E1.justification: v4 retains the four original datasets and adds reported classification results on Caltech-101, CIFAR-100, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets, STL-10, ImageNet, and small NORB. Small NORB introduces controlled lighting shifts, while Caltech-101 foreground-background segmentation adds a distinct prediction task (Tables 4-7).

E2.justification: The MNIST comparison replaces the reported CEConv-2 hybrid with CEConv-4; the earlier CEConv corresponds to CEConv-3. v4 also adds CEConv-4 on 3D Shapes, CEConv-3 on Camelyon17, and grayscale/color-jitter ResNet baselines in Table 4. Conversely, the ResNet18/44 comparisons in v2's 3D Shapes table disappear. Sorting analyses add ResNet and CEConv comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols include training-fraction sweeps, rotation-restoration and relative-equivariance measurements, lighting-based NORB splits, and segmentation with a 6941/868/868 split and 224-by-224 resizing. The CIFAR-10 description changes from 40k training/10k validation/10k testing to 50k training/10k testing in v4 Appendix D.4, although that paragraph calls the dataset CIFAR-100. This documents an inconsistent setting revision, without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 adds sample-efficiency analysis, rotation invertibility versus group order, quantitative equivariance error, expanded CEConv feature-map/sorting comparisons, and hospital saturation distributions (Figures 3, 4, 6, 18; Appendix B). However, most saturation-step sensitivity rows from v2's Camelyon17 and CIFAR-10 tables disappear, despite retained prose mentioning four discretizations.

E5.justification: The original three-seed MNIST/3D Shapes/CIFAR-10 and five-seed Camelyon17 reporting remains unchanged. v4 explicitly discloses one ImageNet seed, 1999, and introduces plots with shaded bands and error bars. It does not document increased repetitions for the original experiments or clearly specify run counts for every added dataset.

E6.justification: Many original scores persist, including Camelyon17's 16.08 (2.68), now labeled Sat-3. Major additions include NORB A/B errors of 18.45 for Lum-3 versus 37.70 for ResNet18, ImageNet Hue-3 error of 30.28, and segmentation errors of 9.67 versus 11.25 (Tables 5-7). New sample-efficiency and equivariance findings substantially expand the results. Some retained entries also change, including MNIST Hue-3's parenthesized A/B variability from 0.28 to 0.29.

T1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds definitions of the luminance group and its image/feature-map actions, following the existing saturation construction. The original hue/saturation proofs move from v2 Appendix C to v4 Appendix A with essentially unchanged reasoning, and the lifting-equivariance derivation is retained. The formal expansion is limited.

C1.justification: v2 foregrounds hue/saturation equivariance, comparable parameter counts, and on-par or better classification. v4 adds central claims of luminance equivariance, improved sample efficiency, stability across hue discretizations, and over three orders of magnitude lower equivariance error than CEConv. Its abstract also claims consistent outperformance of competitive baselines.

C2.justification: v4 develops the earlier brief invalid-RGB observation into a projection/invertibility explanation, identifies the N=1 and N=3 exceptions, and attributes CEConv-4's poorer generalization to equivariance error. It removes v2's explicit lack-of-luminance-equivariance limitation after introducing luminance models. Computational and finite-discretization limitations remain, with a more concrete computational-cost explanation.

D1.justification: v4 adds a source-code availability statement and repository link, training recipes for added benchmarks, ImageNet's eight-GPU hardware configuration, and Stanford Cars reconstruction resources. Appendix E.3 and Table 8 document mask preparation and the segmentation backbone layer by layer. These substantially expand reproducibility information, while most original training recipes remain.

R1.justification: The established equivariant-network literature and closest predecessor, CEConv, remain central. v4 refines the distinction from CEConv by dropping the fully-equivariant-versus-hybrid novelty claim and adding luminance. Supporting citations include Elesedy on sample efficiency, Zhdanov et al. on equivariance measurement, and additional dataset/implementation references. CEConv's corrected bibliography represents the same prior work.

P1.justification: Beyond the title and author-presentation changes, v4 substantially rewrites the abstract, contribution framing, and experimental narrative around CEConv, sample efficiency, and equivariance error. Dataset descriptions move into appendices, which are reorganized from datasets/training/proofs into proofs, comparisons, datasets, implementation, and additional results.

P2.justification: The two-column presentation becomes a single-column ICLR layout. v2 Figures 1 and 2 are combined into v4 Figure 1, Table 4 becomes a six-dataset comparison, and color-sorting displays expand into multiple-model comparisons. New diagnostic, luminance, and segmentation figures and tables substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for the central lifting-layer advantage: the earlier mainly N=3/hybrid CEConv comparison gains matched N=4 comparisons and quantitative invertibility/equivariance analyses. Luminance and segmentation experiments test previously unsupported capabilities, while added controls and implementation information improve evaluability. These gains outweigh the removed sensitivity rows and remaining documentation problems. Qualifications remain: the CIFAR split is inconsistent, and the broad outperformance language exceeds Table 4's mixed results against conventional ResNet.
